verses.text: Bel bows down. Nebo stoops. Their idols are carried by animals, and on the livestock. The things that you carried around are heavy loads, a burden for the weary.
They stoop and they bow down together. They could not deliver the burden, but they have gone into captivity.
“Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, that have been carried from their birth, that have been carried from the womb.
Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear. Yes, I will carry, and will deliver.
“To whom will you liken me, and consider my equal, and compare me, that we may be equal?
Some pour out gold from the bag, and weigh silver in the balance. They hire a goldsmith, and he makes it a god. They fall down — yes, they worship.

They bear it on their shoulder. They carry it, and set it in its place, and it stands there. It cannot move from its place. Yes, one may cry to it, yet it can not answer. It cannot save him out of his trouble.
“Remember this, and show yourselves men. Bring it to mind again, you transgressors.
Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is no other. I am God, and there is none like me.
I declare the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things that are not yet done. I say: My counsel will stand, and I will do all that I please.
I call a ravenous bird from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. Yes, I have spoken. I will also bring it to pass. I have planned. I will also do it.
Listen to me, you stubborn-hearted, who are far from righteousness!
I bring my righteousness near. It is not far off, and my salvation will not wait. I will grant salvation to Zion, my glory to Israel.

footnotes.content: The gods of Babylon themselves must be carried by beasts. How telling—what claims divinity yet needs livestock to move it? Here is the deepest comfort: the Lord who calls us is not a thing to be hauled; He is the One who does the carrying.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Both the gods and their worshippers stoop together and go into captivity. They cannot save themselves, let alone those who bow to them. The idols fall silent. But not so with the God of Israel—His silence is never abandonment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Carried from the womb"—what intimacy. The Lord speaks of His people as He knows them from the beginning, as a mother knows the child she bears. Even when Israel feels small and lost, they are *known* and *already held* in those ancient arms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Even to old age I am he." The promise echoes across decades, even when we turn gray and weary. The Lord does not retire from carrying us; He promises it is *He* who will bear and deliver to the end. Old age is not abandonment—it is His most tender proving ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A simple question becomes an invitation: "To whom will you liken me?" Not in pride, but as the only honest answer. When we have finally looked everywhere else, we turn to see there is no comparison. And perhaps that is when we truly begin to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold weighed and shaped into false gods—precious stuff corrupted into emptiness. How many things we polish and call divine, only to find they answer nothing. The Lord sees our hunger for worship; He grieves when we feed it with what cannot satisfy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An idol needs shoulders to bear it, hands to set it down. It cannot move, cannot hear, cannot save. How much effort we pour into gods that cannot lift a finger to help. Yet the real God carries *us* without us having to shoulder Him first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Show yourselves men"—recall who you truly are. The call to remember is the call to repent, to stand up straight and face what is real. The Lord does not shame us; He invites us to the dignity of the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am God, and there is no other." A declaration so plain it cannot be argued, yet somehow it still takes a lifetime to believe it in our bones. This is the still point around which all else moves. There is no other.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord declares what will be before time draws it into sight. Our tomorrow is His "already." This is not fortune-telling or cosmic fate—it is the deep rest of knowing our future rests in hands wiser than our own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The eagle from the east—likely referring to Cyrus, though we may not yet see it. The Lord has already called what will come to pass. We are invited to trust not the visible alone, but the word spoken long before the wings appeared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Stubborn-hearted" and "far from righteousness"—a diagnosis honest enough to break us open if we let it. But this verse is not condemnation; it is the beginning of restoration. The Lord speaks to us *in* our distance, calling us home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: righteousness is not something we must sprint to find, but something the Lord brings *near*. In a time when we feel far, He draws close. Salvation does not tarry—it arrives because He has determined it, for Zion, for all who call Him Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
